title: Lethbridge Home Rebates 2026: CEIP Is Full for Now
desc: Lethbridge home rebates for 2026: the City's CEIP offers a 2.83% fixed rate and a $1,350 rebate but is at capacity and closed to pre-qualification. What else exists and what ended.
lead: Lethbridge has one of the better local offers in Alberta on paper: a 2.83% fixed rate and a $1,350 rebate through the City's CEIP. Right now it is at capacity and closed to pre-qualification, so for most of Lethbridge's 40,225 households the practical help is small.
cards_heading: What is open for Lethbridge homes in 2026
cards_intro: We re-read each program page on October 3, 2026. Alberta has no provincial home rebates, so the help is local financing and a few small offers.

cards.title: Lethbridge CEIP
cards.note: Financing repaid on your property tax bill, with a $1,350 rebate. The program is at capacity and closed to pre-qualification. Applicants already queued are handled first come, first served.

cards.title: Utility rebates
cards.note: We found no primary source for a current ENMAX, ATCO, EPCOR or FortisAlberta heat pump or solar rebate, so we show none. Ask your utility before you buy.

cards.title: Federal Oil to Heat Pump Affordability
cards.note: The federal program for oil-heated homes stopped taking Alberta applications after July 31, 2026.

cards.title: Canada Greener Homes Grant and Loan
cards.note: The grant's document deadline was December 31, 2025 and the loan cannot approve new applications.

cards.title: Greener Homes Affordability Program
cards.note: Alberta is not among the provinces taking part, as of August 31, 2026.

sections: Lethbridge has 40,225 households. About 63% live in detached houses, 6% in row homes, 6% in semi-detached homes and 8% in duplexes, with only 2% in buildings of five or more storeys. Owners make up 68% and renters 32%. It is a low-rise city, which suits a property-tax-bill loan.

CEIP lends against the property and is repaid on the tax bill, so the debt stays with the house if you sell. Lethbridge pairs its loan with a $1,350 rebate. The fixed rate is 2.83%, lower than Edmonton's 6.00%. The catch is capacity: the City is not taking pre-qualifications now, and people already in the queue go first. Check the City's page for when it reopens.

Lethbridge's average January low is -8.1°C, milder than northern Alberta, though the coldest day in our records reached -37.0°C. About 45% of homes were built before 1981. Southern Alberta's milder average makes a heat pump a more comfortable fit than in Fort McMurray, but the rebate for one is not available.

We looked for a current heat pump or solar rebate from the utilities serving Alberta cities and found no primary source. Do not assume one exists because a neighbour mentioned it. Ask your electricity provider and keep any reply.

The federal oil-to-heat-pump program stopped taking Alberta applications after July 31, 2026. The Greener Homes grant and loan are closed, and Alberta is not in the Greener Homes Affordability Program.
Questions to ask before you sign

If a contractor mentions the Lethbridge CEIP, ask three things. Is the project already pre-qualified, since the City is not accepting new ones? Does the quote assume the $1,350 rebate, and if so on what date will it apply? Is the quote valid long enough to wait for the next intake? A price that depends on a program you cannot yet enter is a price that can change.

Our climate data gives an average January low of -8.1°C and a record low of -37.0°C. Those figures say nothing about wind, which we have no sourced measure for, so we do not rank Lethbridge against other cities on it. For any envelope work, ask the contractor how they test for air leakage before and after.
claim_steps: Check the City's CEIP page for when pre-qualification reopens.
Get quotes in the meantime, asking each to name any rebate it assumes.
Ask your electricity provider about any current offer and keep the reply.
Compare the 2.83% rate with your own financing.
Keep invoices for any future program.
